title: Climate Tipping Points
scope: Thresholds in the Earth system that trigger self-perpetuating change.

overview.summary: Whether warming is pushing ice sheets, forests, reefs and ocean currents past points of no return, and what that should mean for climate policy.
overview.scope_covered: Where the tipping thresholds lie for ice sheets, reefs, forests, permafrost and Atlantic currents; how close warming has come; how fast change follows once one is crossed; whether an overshoot can be reversed; how tipping risk should shape targets.
overview.scope_excluded: The general pace of emissions cuts, carbon removal, solar geoengineering governance in general, societal collapse and wildfires, except where a camp’s case on tipping depends on them. Positive tipping points in technology appear only as a strategy.
overview.why_now: On August 13, 2026, Utrecht University researchers reported in Nature Climate Change that the Atlantic overturning circulation’s tipping point depends on how fast the world warms: in their model it held to 5.5°C when carbon dioxide rose slowly but collapsed near 2°C when it rose at today’s rate.
overview.why_now_source_label: Nature Climate Change, van Westen, Börner and Dijkstra

stats.label: Warming at which each tipping element is estimated to tip
stats.note: Central estimates put the threshold for coral reefs at 1.2°C of warming, Greenland and West Antarctica at 1.5°C and the Amazon at 3.5°C; each spans a wide range, and newer studies put some lower.
stats.detail: These are the central estimates of the Global Tipping Points Report 2023 or, where it made no update, of Armstrong McKay and colleagues’ 2022 assessment in Science, as tabulated in a February 2026 review by 28 researchers. Warming is measured against 1850–1900. The ranges matter as much as the central figures: coral reefs 1.0 to 1.5°C, Greenland 0.8 to 3.0, West Antarctica 1.0 to 3.0, permafrost 1.0 to 2.3, the subpolar gyre 1.1 to 3.8, mountain glaciers 1.5 to 3.0, the West African monsoon 2.0 to 3.5, the Amazon 2.0 to 6.0, the boreal forest 1.4 to 5.0 and the Atlantic overturning circulation 1.4 to 8.0. Some estimates have since moved: a May 2026 Nature study put the Amazon’s threshold at 1.5 to 1.9°C once deforestation is counted. The 2022 assessment concluded that six tipping points become likely, and four more possible, within the Paris Agreement range of 1.5 to under 2°C.
stats.source_label: Ritchie, Steinert et al., Environmental Research Letters 21 (2026), Table 1

stats.label: Global warming in 2025
stats.note: The world was 1.39°C warmer in 2025 than in 1850–1900, an estimated 1.37°C of it caused by people, and human-caused warming is rising by about 0.27°C per decade.
stats.detail: The yearly figure moves with the weather: 2024 was 1.51°C, the first calendar year above 1.5°C, and 2025 was cooler because of a weak La Niña. The average for 2016–2025 was 1.26°C, and the authors project that human-induced warming will reach 1.5°C around 2030 at current emissions. The Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C refers to a long-term average, so a single year above it does not breach the goal. The tipping thresholds are expressed on the same scale, so warming as of 2025 already exceeds the central estimate for coral reefs and sits inside the lower end of the ranges for Greenland, West Antarctica, permafrost and the subpolar gyre.
stats.source_label: Forster et al., Indicators of Global Climate Change 2025, Earth System Science Data 18 (2026)

stats.label: Years for a tipping element to change once past its threshold
stats.note: Once past its threshold, coral reefs are estimated to shift within about a decade, the Atlantic circulation in about 50 years, the Amazon in a century and Greenland’s ice over about 10,000 years.
stats.detail: These are central estimates with wide ranges: the Atlantic overturning circulation 15 to 300 years, the West Antarctic ice sheet 500 to 13,000, Greenland 1,000 to 15,000. Timescale is what separates two readings of the same threshold table. To one side, a threshold crossed now commits future generations to losses that cannot be undone on any human timescale. To the other, “tipping” is a misleading word for changes that play out over centuries or millennia and remain partly avoidable.
stats.source_label: Ritchie, Steinert et al., Environmental Research Letters 21 (2026), Table 1

stats.label: Chance of triggering tipping points under current-policy warming
stats.note: On the emissions path closest to current policies, a 2025 study’s most conservative estimate is a 62 percent chance of triggering, averaged over 16 tipping elements; nine top even odds.
stats.detail: Triggering means a threshold is crossed at some point along the warming path, not that the change finishes this century; for ice sheets the consequences would unfold over centuries to millennia. On this middle-of-the-road pathway (SSP2-4.5), Barents Sea ice, the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, abrupt permafrost thaw and coral reefs were triggered with more than 90 percent probability, while the Atlantic overturning circulation stayed below 50 percent and East Antarctica below 10 percent. The same paper found that carbon released by Amazon dieback and permafrost thaw adds relatively little warming, on average about a tenth of human-caused warming or less, raising the average triggering probability by at most 3 percentage points. Lower-emissions pathways cut the risk substantially.
stats.source_label: Deutloff, Held and Lenton, Earth System Dynamics 16 (2025)

stats.label: Tipping elements expected to tip if warming holds at each level
stats.note: If warming were held at 1.5°C with no overshoot, it is as likely as not that three tipping elements would tip; at 2°C, five; at 3°C, eight would likely tip.
stats.detail: The review uses the IPCC’s probability language: “as likely as not” means a 33 to 66 percent chance and “likely” means above 66 percent. At 1.5°C one of the three is warm-water coral reefs, which the authors call “virtually certain” to tip because the top of their threshold range is 1.5°C; the other two could be any combination of the North Atlantic subpolar gyre, land permafrost and the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets. At 2°C the candidates widen to include mountain glaciers, boreal forests and the Atlantic overturning circulation. “Tip” here means the threshold is crossed for long enough to commit the system to change, not that the change is complete; for ice sheets it would unfold over thousands of years.
stats.source_label: Ritchie, Steinert et al., Environmental Research Letters 21 (2026), section 3 and figure 3

stats.label: Coral reef area hit by bleaching-level heat stress, 2023–2025
stats.note: From January 2023 to September 2025, about 84.4 percent of the world’s coral reef area had heat stress strong enough to bleach coral, the largest global bleaching event on record.
stats.detail: Mass bleaching was documented in at least 83 countries and territories. It was the fourth global bleaching event on record, after 1998, 2010 and 2014–2017, and beat the previous record of 68.2 percent of reef area. NOAA confirmed the event in April 2024 and said in June 2026 that it had likely ended in mid-2025. Heat stress is not death: bleached corals can recover if the water cools in time, and mortality varied widely from reef to reef. The Global Tipping Points Report 2025 used this event to conclude that reefs are passing their tipping point and that functional reefs at a meaningful scale require warming to fall back toward 1°C. Others read the same record as severe, recurring damage from which reefs can partly recover.
stats.source_label: NOAA Coral Reef Watch, Current Global Bleaching status update

stats.label: Chance the 2026–2030 average exceeds 1.5°C
stats.note: The World Meteorological Organization puts a 75 percent chance on the 2026–2030 average exceeding 1.5°C above 1850–1900, and a 91 percent chance on at least one of those years doing so.
stats.detail: A five-year average above 1.5°C is still not the long-term, roughly 20-year average that the Paris Agreement refers to, but it is close. For tipping points, the practical question has therefore shifted from whether 1.5°C will be exceeded to how far and for how long. A return below it after an overshoot depends on first reaching net-zero emissions and then removing carbon from the air at scale.
stats.source_label: World Meteorological Organization, Global Annual to Decadal Climate Update 2026–2035

stats.label: Amazon forest lost to deforestation
stats.note: The Amazon has lost about 13 percent of its original forest, or 15 percent counting young secondary forest, beyond the 10 percent a 2024 study proposes as a safe limit.
stats.detail: The Amazon recycles much of its own rain: moisture evaporated by trees in the east falls again further west, so clearing forest dries the forest downwind. Past a point, that feedback could turn large areas into degraded forest or savanna, and one model found forest loss accelerating at about 20 percent deforestation. Flores and colleagues, 24 authors in all, proposed safe boundaries of 1.5°C of warming and 10 percent cumulative deforestation, which would require ending large-scale clearing and restoring at least 5 percent of the biome. Beyond the forest cleared outright, about 38 percent of what remains has been degraded by logging, fire, edge effects and drought, and the southeastern Amazon has already become a net source of carbon.
stats.source_label: Flores et al., Critical transitions in the Amazon forest system, Nature 626 (2024)

stats.label: Warming projected by 2100
stats.note: Governments’ current policies put the world on track for about 2.6°C of warming by 2100; meeting every announced target, including net-zero pledges, would bring it to about 1.9°C.
stats.detail: The current-policy projection has fallen from about 3.6°C in 2015 but has changed little since 2021; the 0.1°C improvement in 2025 came mainly from a change in how China’s long-term emissions are modeled. Against the threshold estimates, a 2.6°C world lies beyond the central figures for coral reefs, Greenland, West Antarctica, permafrost, the subpolar gyre and mountain glaciers, and within the ranges for the Amazon, the boreal forest and the Atlantic overturning circulation.
stats.source_label: Climate Action Tracker, Global Update, 13 November 2025

stats.label: Projected weakening of the Atlantic overturning circulation by 2100
stats.note: Corrected against observed temperature and salinity, models project the Atlantic circulation weakening 51 ± 8 percent by 2100 on a middle emissions path, against 32 ± 37 percent uncorrected.
stats.detail: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) carries warm surface water north through the Atlantic and returns cold water south at depth; it keeps northwestern Europe mild and shapes monsoon rainfall in Africa and Asia. A weakening is not a collapse, but a weaker circulation is closer to the point where it could stop sustaining itself. The IPCC’s 2021 assessment said the AMOC is “very likely to weaken over the 21st century” but gave “medium confidence that there will not be an abrupt collapse before 2100.” Estimates of collapse risk vary widely: a 2023 statistical study projected a transition most likely around 2057, with a 95 percent interval of 2037 to 2109 after a 2025 correction; a 2025 multi-model study in Nature found collapse this century unlikely; and a June 2026 preprint, not peer reviewed at the time, put a 10 to 23 percent probability on collapse already being committed.

stats.label: Share of the Amazon forest at risk of transition
stats.note: Without deforestation, a 2026 model finds up to about a third of the Amazon losing stability past 3.7 to 4.0°C; with 22 to 28 percent deforestation, 62 to 77 percent transitions at 1.5 to 1.9°C.
stats.detail: The study couples a model of how moisture travels across the Amazon basin with a model of forest stability, so drying in one place can push forest downwind past its own threshold. Most of the simulated transitions come from these knock-on effects, which the authors describe as self-propelling cascades over hundreds to thousands of kilometers. That is why the consensus Amazon threshold and this study’s differ so much: the lower number assumes deforestation continues, rising in the scenario used from about 18 percent of the basin in 2020 to 35 percent in 2050. The authors conclude that warming should be kept below 1.5°C, deforestation halted and degraded forests restored.
stats.source_label: Wunderling et al., Deforestation-induced drying lowers Amazon climate threshold, Nature (6 May 2026)

stats.label: Sea-level rise held in each ice sheet
stats.note: Fully melted, Greenland’s ice sheet would raise global sea level by about 7.4 meters and Antarctica’s, the far larger of the two, by about 58.
stats.detail: Ice-sheet tipping is the slowest and largest of the tipping elements. Greenland’s feedback is gradual: as the ice surface melts and lowers, it sits in warmer air and melts faster. West Antarctica’s risk comes from marine ice-sheet instability, in which ice resting on bedrock below sea level retreats faster once warm ocean water gets beneath it. Crossing a threshold commits the world to this rise only over centuries to millennia. The IPCC’s 2021 assessment found “limited evidence for low-likelihood, high-impact outcomes” that would strongly increase Antarctic ice loss for centuries under high emissions.
stats.source_label: National Snow and Ice Data Center, Ice sheet quick facts

stats.label: Ice lost by the great ice sheets each year, 2002–2025
stats.note: Satellite gravity measurements show Greenland losing about 266 billion tonnes of ice a year and Antarctica about 135 billion tonnes a year since 2002.
stats.detail: Both ice sheets are losing mass, and their losses are a growing share of sea-level rise. Losing mass is not the same as having tipped: a shrinking ice sheet can stabilize if warming stops, and the open question is whether parts of Greenland or West Antarctica have already passed the point where retreat continues regardless. The IPCC judged continued ice loss over the 21st century virtually certain for Greenland and likely for Antarctica. The measurements come from the GRACE and GRACE Follow-On satellites, which track changes in Earth’s gravity.

stats.label: Carbon stored in Arctic soils and permafrost
stats.note: At least 1.4 to 1.6 trillion tonnes of carbon have built up in northern permafrost soils, and NOAA reported in 2024 that the Arctic tundra, counting wildfires, had become a net source of CO2.
stats.detail: Only part of the permafrost store could thaw this century, and much of what thaws would be released slowly. Estimates of the extra warming from permafrost and other carbon feedbacks are generally in tenths of a degree by 2100. Abrupt thaw, in which ground ice melts and the land surface collapses, is listed as a tipping element with a threshold of about 1.5°C, and its emissions are not fully included in most climate models. Circumpolar wildfires have emitted an average of 207 million tonnes of carbon a year since 2003.
stats.source_label: NOAA Arctic Report Card 2024, Arctic Terrestrial Carbon Cycling

stats.label: Remaining CO2 budget from 2026, for an even chance of each limit
stats.note: For an even chance of holding warming to 1.5°C, the world can emit about 130 billion more tonnes of CO2 from the start of 2026, a little over three years at 2025’s rate of 42 billion tonnes.
stats.detail: The budgets count only uncertainty in how warming responds to CO2; they would shrink with a higher required confidence or larger feedbacks. The 2°C budget, about 1,050 billion tonnes, is roughly 25 years of emissions at the 2025 rate. The figure matters for tipping because the thresholds cluster at 1.5 to 2°C: the size of what remains decides whether avoiding them means cutting emissions or, after an overshoot, removing carbon to bring temperatures back down. The 1.5°C budget has fallen by about 370 billion tonnes since the IPCC’s 2021 estimate, which counted from 2020.
stats.source_label: Forster et al., Indicators of Global Climate Change 2025, Earth System Science Data 18 (2026), Table 8

stats.label: How much tipping points add to the social cost of carbon
stats.note: Eight tipping points raised a model’s expected social cost of carbon 24.5 percent, mostly via methane hydrates and permafrost; AMOC slowdown and sea-ice albedo slightly lower it. Some call it a floor, others a ceiling.
stats.detail: The social cost of carbon is the estimated damage from emitting one more tonne of CO2, used to weigh climate policy against its costs. In this model it rose from about $52 to $65 per tonne, and the authors estimate about a 10 percent chance that tipping points more than double it. The AMOC slowdown pulls the other way because a weaker circulation cools Europe and offsets some warming damage there. The authors call the result “a probable underestimate,” because the literature they synthesized does not cover all tipping points and the main specification leaves out non-market damages such as ecosystems and health; other economists argued in PNAS that such models understate tipping damages by far more. A 2025 review written for the US Department of Energy cited the same study against large revisions to the social cost of carbon, noting that the IPCC considers the methane-hydrate scenario very unlikely.
stats.source_label: Dietz, Rising, Stoerk and Wagner, Economic impacts of tipping points in the climate system, PNAS 118 (2021), Table 1

stats.label: Hard coral cover on the Great Barrier Reef, by region
stats.note: After near-record highs in 2024, hard coral cover on the Great Barrier Reef fell sharply in 2025 after mass bleaching, then rose in the north and center in 2026 while slipping slightly in the south.
stats.detail: The 2025 surveys found the largest single-year declines in two of the three regions since monitoring began 39 years earlier, and the Australian Institute of Marine Science described a reef with “increased volatility.” The 2026 figures come from surveys of 121 reefs between August 2025 and June 2026, and AIMS said in 2026 that cover remained close to its 40-year averages. The Great Barrier Reef is one reef system among many and is better protected than most. Its record is read both ways: as evidence that reefs recover faster than tipping-point language implies, and as evidence that fast-growing corals now boom and bust with each marine heatwave, a pattern that shortens recovery time as bleaching grows more frequent.
stats.source_label: Australian Institute of Marine Science, Long-Term Monitoring Program annual summaries 2024/25 and 2025/26 (via GCRMN)

stats.label: Share of new cars sold worldwide that were electric, 2025
stats.note: One in four new cars sold worldwide in 2025 was electric, more than 20 million in all; in China the share was close to 55 percent.
stats.detail: Electric cars are the headline example of what some researchers call a positive tipping point: a threshold, usually cost parity, past which a clean technology spreads under its own momentum as prices fall and infrastructure grows. The Global Tipping Points Report 2025 said such points have already been crossed in solar and wind power worldwide and in electric vehicles, batteries and heat pumps in leading markets. The International Energy Agency notes that growth slowed in China in 2025.
stats.source_label: International Energy Agency, Global EV Outlook 2026

questions.text: Are the major tipping thresholds within reach of this century’s warming?
questions.why: Threshold estimates span several degrees and rest on ancient climate records, models that disagree and expert judgment. Small shifts in the lower bound turn “tipping now” into “tipping unlikely this century.”
questions.detail:
Those who see them within reach note that today’s warming already passes the coral reefs’ central estimate and falls inside the low end of several other ranges, and that the path set by current policies runs well beyond them. New studies keep moving thresholds down, for the Amazon when deforestation is counted and for the Atlantic circulation when warming is fast. Observations back the models: record bleaching, a weakening Atlantic circulation, shrinking ice sheets and a tundra that now releases more carbon than it absorbs.

Those who see them mostly out of reach note that the systems with the largest global consequences, the Atlantic circulation, an intact Amazon and East Antarctica, have central thresholds beyond current-policy warming. The lowest estimates come from single models, statistical extrapolation or preprints that have not been peer reviewed. Reefs damaged by heat still recover in places, and ice sheets that cross a threshold take centuries to millennia to respond, which leaves time for warming to be reversed.

questions.text: Should the risk of tipping points set the level of climate targets?
questions.why: Some read tipping points as cliffs in the damage curve that call for precaution; others would price them like any other risk. Which to steer by is a choice about acting under deep uncertainty.
questions.detail:
For those who would let thresholds set targets, a loss that is irreversible on any human timescale, such as meters of sea-level rise or the Amazon, breaks the ordinary logic of trading damages against costs, because the damages cannot be undone once the costs are known. Economic models that add tipping points raise the cost of carbon and carry a long tail in which it more than doubles, and those models leave out much of what would be lost.

For those who would let costs and benefits set targets, climate policy has real costs, borne disproportionately by poorer people now, and thresholds whose ranges run several degrees wide cannot anchor a line. Weighing tipping as one risk among many, priced alongside the others, avoids spending on the wrong things in a panic and keeps money for measures that pay off whatever happens.

questions.text: Can a temporary overshoot of 1.5°C be reversed before tipping takes hold?
questions.why: Warming is expected to pass 1.5°C, so whether a return is possible matters for every target. The answer depends on how far and how long the overshoot runs, and on carbon removal at a scale no one had reached as of 2026.
questions.detail:
Those who think an overshoot recoverable note that ice sheets and other slow elements take centuries to millennia to respond, so briefly crossing their thresholds need not commit them; a February 2026 review of overshoot states that “tipping does not always occur immediately.” Warming largely stops within a few years of reaching net-zero CO2, and net-negative emissions can then bring temperatures down. Planning for a managed overshoot and return, rather than pretending 1.5°C can still be held, gives policy a target it can meet.

Those who think it too risky note that fast elements such as coral reefs, and possibly the subpolar gyre and the Atlantic circulation, can tip within the overshoot itself. The August 2026 Utrecht study found the Atlantic circulation’s stability depends on the rate of warming, so a fast rise can set off collapse even if temperatures later fall. A return requires removing hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2, which was not possible at scale as of 2026, and a 2025 study found the overshoot behavior of tipping elements “still highly uncertain.”

questions.text: Is “tipping point” the right way to describe how these systems change?
questions.why: The term comes from systems where a small push flips one stable state into another. Critics say many listed elements respond in proportion to warming over long timescales, and that the word implies a speed and finality the physics does not show.
questions.detail:
Those who see real thresholds point to abrupt shifts in the climate record, such as the rapid coolings and warmings of the last ice age linked to the Atlantic circulation, and the greening and drying of the Sahara. The feedbacks are well-understood physics: melt lowers an ice surface into warmer air, forest loss cuts the rain that sustains the rest of the forest, fresher water reduces the sinking that drives ocean circulation. Early-warning signals, such as rising variance and slower recovery from disturbances, have been detected in the Amazon, Greenland and the Atlantic circulation.

Those who see gradual slopes note that permafrost, mountain glaciers and summer sea ice respond roughly in proportion to warming, and that even the threshold elements change over decades to millennia. On this reading, describing damage degree by degree is both more accurate and more useful for planning, and still leaves room for the few systems with genuine thresholds.

questions.text: Would tipping in one system trigger tipping in others?
questions.why: The systems are linked: Greenland meltwater weakens the Atlantic circulation, which shifts rainfall over the Amazon and West Africa. Whether those links make a chain reaction likely, or are small next to human emissions, is unsettled.
questions.detail:
Those who expect cascades cite the 2018 “Hothouse Earth” paper, which argued that linked feedbacks could push the planet onto a hotter path no longer driven by human emissions, and network studies since that find interactions lower the effective thresholds of many elements. Within the Amazon, knock-on drying spreads forest loss far downwind, and a June 2026 preprint found that the chance of an Atlantic collapse already being committed depends on how much Greenland is melting.

Those who see the systems as mostly independent note that the largest links act over centuries, and that carbon from Amazon dieback and permafrost thaw adds only a small fraction of human-caused warming. Some links stabilize: a weaker Atlantic circulation cools the North Atlantic, which may slow Greenland’s melt. The climate scientist Andrew Dessler wrote in March 2026 that a true runaway greenhouse “is simply not in the cards on any time horizon we care about,” and a 2023 review found emissions pathways and model uncertainty may matter more than tipping elements for multi-century warming.

questions.text: Should governments research ways to cool the climate or hold back specific tipping points?
questions.why: Reflecting sunlight, brightening clouds or thickening sea ice might buy time for particular systems, but each carries its own risks, could distract from emissions cuts and raises the question of who decides for the planet.
questions.detail:
Those who favor research argue that if some tipping points are already being crossed and emissions cuts cannot reverse warming quickly, the only way to protect those systems in time may be to act on them directly, and that any decision about such tools should rest on evidence rather than guesswork. Leaving them unstudied, on this view, only guarantees that a desperate future choice is made blind.

Those who would rule them out cite a September 2025 assessment by 42 polar scientists that five proposed polar geoengineering concepts are environmentally dangerous and unworkable at the needed scale. Solar geoengineering would have to be kept up for decades or centuries, could shift monsoons and rainfall, and would bring “termination shock” if stopped. Research lends it legitimacy, may weaken the pressure to cut emissions, and has no governance system to decide on deployment; some scholars and governments favor a non-use agreement.

questions.text: Can “positive tipping points” in technology and society move fast enough to matter?
questions.why: Supporters say clean technologies spread through reinforcing feedbacks, so small policy pushes can set off large shifts. Critics say adoption rests on subsidies, politics and infrastructure that can stall or reverse.
questions.detail:
Those who expect self-reinforcing change note that solar and wind are now the cheapest new power in most of the world and that electric car sales have grown faster than most forecasts. A September 2026 report by the University of Exeter and the Earthshot Prize identified 51 solutions that could reach self-propelling change within five years. Targeted mandates and cost parity can tip whole markets, which is faster than persuading every consumer.

Those who expect slow and reversible change note that global emissions are still rising and that current policies still lead well past 2°C. Electric car sales in the United States stayed just under 10 percent and dropped when tax credits ended, a sign that adoption can hang on subsidies that can be withdrawn. Steel, cement, aviation, shipping and farming have no clean option at cost parity, and a shift that looks self-reinforcing in one market can stall in another.

positions.name: Cut emissions fast enough to stay below tipping thresholds
positions.steelman: Some thresholds are already at hand, and what tips cannot be untipped. Cutting too fast costs money we can recover; cutting too slowly loses what is gone for millennia.
positions.detail:
The Earth system has thresholds, and we are at them. Each of these systems, once tipped, commits the world to losses no later policy can reverse: meters of sea-level rise, the end of reefs that feed hundreds of millions, a drying Amazon, a colder, stormier Europe and failed monsoons. Uncertainty cuts both ways: the ranges reach below the central estimates as well as above them, and when the downside is irreversible, uncertainty is a reason for more caution, not less. So the thresholds, not a cost-benefit curve, should set the targets. A February 2026 review by researchers from Exeter, Potsdam and Oslo concludes that warming must peak below 2°C, return below 1.5°C within this century and settle near 1°C thereafter to limit tipping risks. That means halving emissions this decade, phasing out fossil fuels, ending deforestation and building the capacity to draw carbon down.

Most tipping would unfold slowly, which is what makes the next decade decisive: it is when the commitments are made. The message is not that it is too late; each increment of warming avoided lowers the odds. The same reinforcing feedbacks that tip the Earth also spread clean technology, and solar, wind and electric vehicles have already passed their own tipping points in leading markets. Some of us stress the rate of warming as well as its peak; others put most weight on triggering more of these positive tipping points.
positions.proponents: Global Tipping Points Report; University of Exeter Global Systems Institute; Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research; Stockholm Resilience Centre; Timothy Lenton; Paul Ritchie; Nico Wunderling

positions.name: Weigh tipping risks by expected cost and build resilience
positions.steelman: Climate risk is real, but thresholds nobody can locate should not run policy. Weigh them with costs and benefits like any other risk, and make societies richer and more resilient.
positions.detail:
Climate change is real and some of its risks are serious, but policy should be set by weighing costs against benefits, and tipping points change that arithmetic less than the headlines suggest. When economists add them to their models, most of the increase comes from scenarios the IPCC itself judges very unlikely. What counts as a tipping point is a moving target, from 10 systems to more than 25, and the thresholds are guesses with ranges several degrees wide. The IPCC has medium confidence that the Atlantic circulation will not collapse this century and found no tipping point in Arctic sea ice. Meanwhile the policies justified by emergency language are expensive, fall hardest on poor people and poor countries, and are often ineffective. Predictions of imminent collapse, such as the obituaries for the Great Barrier Reef, keep failing, and as Bjørn Lomborg put it in September 2026, “crying wolf has a well-known ending.”

The objection is that a cost-benefit model cannot price irreversible catastrophe. But steering by the lowest plausible threshold gives no stopping rule and already demands the impossible for coral reefs. Deep uncertainty is not a license to assume the worst. If abrupt changes cannot be predicted, the US Department of Energy’s 2025 climate review concluded, “the most appropriate stance for economic policy is to maximize resilience”: wealth, sea defenses, crop research and cheaper energy, which pay off whatever happens. We range from those who doubt warming will be large to those who accept mainstream projections but favor a moderate carbon price and heavy spending on clean-energy research.
positions.proponents: US Department of Energy Climate Working Group; Judith Curry; Steven Koonin; Ross McKitrick; John Christy; Roy Spencer; Bjørn Lomborg

positions.name: Describe climate risk in degrees, not tipping points
positions.steelman: We take large, hard-to-reverse changes seriously, which is why we describe them precisely. Every tenth of a degree matters, and most of these systems slide rather than fall off a cliff.
positions.detail:
Most of these systems do not fall off a cliff, and even those that could would take centuries to millennia to respond. The word “tipping” implies a single line, a sudden fall and a point of no return, and people hear it either as “it’s too late” or as a deadline that, once missed, discredits the science. It also confuses policy targets like 1.5°C, which are choices, with properties of the climate system. Robert Kopp and nine coauthors, several of them IPCC authors, argued in Nature Climate Change in December 2024 that the framing conveys “urgency without fostering a meaningful basis for climate action.” The Breakthrough Institute’s Seaver Wang wrote that the literature “has not identified any approaching global tipping point after which runaway climate change intensifies beyond humanity’s ability to arrest it.”

We do not deny thresholds; we ask that each be described for what it is, with its probability and its timescale. Urgency built on a claimed cliff collapses when the date passes, while urgency built on steadily rising damage lasts. That argues for cutting emissions as fast as practical and for adapting, without fatalism or false precision. We support fast cuts; we doubt a contested metaphor is the best way to win them.
positions.proponents: Robert Kopp; Elisabeth Gilmore; Michael Oppenheimer; Seaver Wang; Breakthrough Institute

positions.name: Research ways to hold off specific tipping points
positions.steelman: Emissions cuts are essential but cannot cool the planet in time for every system. Study the tools that could protect them now, so any future decision rests on evidence.
positions.detail:
CO2 stays in the air for centuries, and warming will overshoot 1.5°C. If the Arctic, the Greenland ice sheet or the Atlantic circulation are close to tipping, the only tools that could act in time are ones that act on those systems directly: brightening clouds over the Arctic, thickening sea ice, shielding glaciers from warm ocean water with underwater curtains, or reflecting a little sunlight. None is ready, and some may prove unworkable or dangerous. That is the reason to research them now, carefully and openly. The UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency has committed £56.8 million to research, including a limited number of small, controlled outdoor experiments, on whether such approaches are feasible and safe.

We agree that most concepts may fail and that none should be deployed without evidence and consent, above all from Arctic peoples. But if research is never done, the world meets a collapse with no options, what John Moore and colleagues call “the moral hazard of non-research.” Research is funded alongside decarbonization, never instead of it. Most of us fund research only and set no deployment plan; the Centre for Climate Repair at Cambridge, which also works to refreeze the Arctic, says eventual deployment decisions “should not be taken unilaterally.”
positions.proponents: Advanced Research and Invention Agency; John Moore; Marc Macias-Fauria; Michael Wolovick; Centre for Climate Repair at Cambridge; David King

positions.name: Prepare communities for societal collapse
positions.steelman: Thirty years of promises have not bent the curve. Some societal breakdown is likely or already here, and honest preparation, local and shared, beats a hope that keeps failing.
positions.detail:
The official story, that warming can still be held to safe levels if we try harder, has been told for thirty years while emissions kept rising. Self-reinforcing feedbacks in the Arctic, in permafrost and in the oceans are under way, and they are converging with crises in energy, food, finance and politics. Honesty requires admitting that some form of societal breakdown is likely or already happening in many places, and that mitigation, still worth doing, will not prevent it. Jem Bendell, whose 2018 paper Deep Adaptation named the movement, writes that “societal collapse is no longer a distant possibility but a lived reality for many.”

The task is to prepare: build local resilience, food and mutual aid, let go of what cannot be kept, and resist the authoritarian responses that crises invite. Critics say the science does not show collapse is inevitable; Bendell revised the paper in 2020 to say it cannot be proven certain, and our case does not rest on certainty. Preparing is prudent if breakdown is likely, and stronger communities are good whether or not it comes. Despair comes from false hope colliding with reality, not from honest acknowledgment.

crux.lead: Is a climate tipping point a cliff to stay clear of, or one more cost to weigh?
crux.lead_highlight: a cliff to stay clear of, or one more cost to weigh
crux.subtitle: Nearly everyone agrees that warming raises the risk of large, lasting changes to ice sheets, forests and ocean currents. They split over how close, how fast and how final those changes are, and over how much a loss that cannot be undone should outweigh costs paid today.
crux.empirical: Evidence can settle much of the first part: where the thresholds lie and how wide their ranges really are, how fast each system changes once past one, whether a brief overshoot can be reversed in time, whether the speed of warming matters as well as its level, and whether warning signs in ocean currents, forests and ice are real. Watching these systems will narrow the answers within a decade, though some may come only after a line is crossed.
crux.values: No data settles the rest. People differ on how much weight an unlikely but irreversible loss deserves when it falls mostly on people far away or not yet born, against costs that are certain and paid now. Whether to act on the lowest plausible threshold or on the expected value, and whether a vivid frame that may move people beats a precise one that may not, are choices about precaution and fairness across generations.

actions.title: Read the IPCC’s assessment of abrupt change
actions.description: The Summary for Policymakers of the IPCC’s Sixth Assessment Report, Working Group I; its section C.3 sets out what is and is not known about ice-sheet loss, Atlantic collapse and other high-impact outcomes.

actions.title: Explore Carbon Brief’s explainer on the Atlantic overturning circulation
actions.description: An April 2026 interactive explainer that sets the studies predicting collapse of the Atlantic currents beside those finding them resilient, with scientists quoted on each side.

actions.title: Read the Global Tipping Points Report
actions.description: The report by 160 scientists that judged warm-water coral reefs to be passing their tipping point, assesses the other major systems and lays out the policies it argues can avoid them.
actions.for_position: Cut emissions fast enough to stay below tipping thresholds

actions.title: Read the Department of Energy’s review of climate impacts
actions.description: The July 2025 report by the US Department of Energy’s Climate Working Group; section 11.2.4 argues that tipping points do not warrant a much higher social cost of carbon and that policy should aim for resilience.
actions.for_position: Weigh tipping risks by expected cost and build resilience

actions.title: Read the case against the tipping-point frame
actions.description: Kopp and colleagues’ December 2024 perspective in Nature Climate Change, “‘Tipping points’ confuse and can distract from urgent climate action,” which asks for clearer language about specific risks.
actions.for_position: Describe climate risk in degrees, not tipping points

actions.title: Follow ARIA’s Exploring Climate Cooling program
actions.description: The UK research agency’s program testing whether ways to delay or avert tipping points, from thickening Arctic sea ice to reflecting sunlight, are feasible and safe, with its projects and safeguards.
actions.for_position: Research ways to hold off specific tipping points

actions.title: Join the Deep Adaptation Forum
actions.description: A network offering events, a community space and volunteer roles for people preparing, personally and in their communities, for societal disruption and collapse.

actions.title: Lobby for a price on carbon with Citizens’ Climate Lobby
actions.description: A nonpartisan volunteer organization with local chapters that trains members to meet their representatives and press for carbon pricing and faster emissions cuts.
actions.for_position: Cut emissions fast enough to stay below tipping thresholds

actions.title: Weigh the polar geoengineering debate
actions.description: A Frontiers in Science collection that sets the 42-scientist assessment calling polar geoengineering dangerous beside replies arguing that research is a form of harm reduction.

actions.title: Survey coral reefs with Reef Check
actions.description: A citizen-science program that trains divers to monitor reef health with a standard method, adding to the record of how reefs bleach and recover.

primary_image_prompt:
A minimalist flat vector-style icon illustration, in a clean editorial line-art style: one compact coastal scene grouped in the center with wide white margins, nothing touching the edges: a tall ice sheet with a sheer flat-topped front edge as the dominant focal mass on the left half, filled; a medium iceberg floating in front of its foot, overlapping the ice face, filled above and below the waterline; a low rounded hill of rainforest tree crowns rising behind the right side of the ice sheet, partly hidden by it; a small rounded coral clump on the curved sea floor at the lower right, below the water; one long wavy sea surface line crossing the whole scene through the iceberg as the connective element; the sea floor is a gentle curve.

Composition: one dominant focal mass with smaller supporting elements at clearly different scales (big, medium, small); at least one element overlaps another so the scene has depth; the ground is a gentle curve, never a flat line; one connective element runs across the frame to tie the pieces together. A single coherent scene, not a row of separate objects. Centered with generous, even padding.

Style: monoline line art with ONE uniform stroke weight on every element, including the thinnest wisps and lines. Rounded line caps and corners. Confident, slightly bold strokes so it stays legible when small. No fussy internal detail.

Color: a single hue, two tones only. Draw all lines in solid #3f9a6a, and give every major mass a clearly visible soft fill of the same hue at about 15-18% opacity, so the duotone is obviously present rather than white interiors. No other colors, no gradients, no shadows, no 3D, no texture.

Important: NO border, NO frame, NO box or outline around the scene, just the illustration on a plain white background. No text, letters, or numbers. No human figures or faces. Calm, neutral, editorial mood: show the subject plainly, neither celebrating nor warning. Also avoid: thermometers, melting globes, polar bears, flames, wildfire, smokestacks, dripping or melting ice, cracks, warning signs, arrows, dials or gauges, seesaws, dominoes, balls on hills, clocks, dead trees, bleached skeletons, storms, sun.
